segments.title: What would delaying the Washington Treaty until 1927 change?
segments.body: Delaying agreement until 1927 would let construction continue while negotiations remained unsettled. G3s, N3s, Lexingtons and their Japanese contemporaries would provide the new starting point. A later settlement could regulate construction rates and replacement instead of using the original aggregate tonnage limits. Continued orders would preserve industrial capacity and replace much of the First World War fleet before the late 1930s. Smaller wars remain a speculative outcome, and stronger fleets would not guarantee peace.

evidence.note: The five-year delay question and the distinction between historical context and an alternate-history scenario.
Failed negotiations allow construction of the cancelled postwar designs.
The proposed later agreement regulates construction and produces a younger capital fleet.
The smaller-war forecast and uncertainty about Italy's relationship with Germany.

segments.question: What happens if the Washington Naval Treaty is delayed by five years, until 1927?
segments.answerShort: The scenario allows the cancelled postwar capital ships to be built, encourages larger carriers and continued design development, and suggests a later treaty based on construction quotas. Younger fleets and preserved shipbuilding capacity would change the balance of power, although the political consequences remain uncertain.

segments.title: Two new battleships in exchange for four older ships
segments.body: Article II identifies the capital ships each power can retain and requires Britain, the United States and Japan to dispose of other capital ships built or building. The United States can complete two West Virginia-class ships while disposing of North Dakota and Delaware. Britain can construct two new capital ships of no more than 35,000 tons standard displacement and must then dispose of four older ships. Those older vessels had been important components of the fleet at Jutland. Exchanging four of them for two postwar designs reflects the difference in capability between generations, which a simple hull count would conceal.

evidence.note: Article II exceptions and the two-for-four British replacement comparison.

segments.summary: Article II ties new construction to scrapping, with Britain exchanging four older battleships for two postwar ships.

segments.title: National tonnage quotas and fleets of 35,000-ton ships
segments.body: The replacement allowances are 525,000 tons each for Britain and the United States, 315,000 for Japan, and 175,000 each for France and Italy. At 35,000 tons per ship, these totals correspond to fifteen, nine and five ships respectively. These are calculations using the maximum replacement size, rather than exact counts of every retained fleet. The quoted standard displacements are 27,500 tons for the Queen Elizabeth class and 25,750 tons for the Royal Sovereigns. Against those existing ships, a 35,000-ton ceiling looks like a plausible compromise.

evidence.note: Article IV figures, ship-count calculation and comparison with existing British classes.

segments.summary: The national tonnage allowances translate into different fleet sizes when every replacement ship uses the 35,000-ton ceiling.

segments.title: Why 35,000 tons excludes the emerging postwar generation
segments.body: Hood's standard displacement is 41,200 tons, while many new capital-ship designs approach 40,000 tons. Most older British ships remain well below the treaty ceiling, including Tiger. A 35,000-ton limit therefore fits the inherited fleet better than the ships being designed around wartime experience. The Washington Cherries are the lost generation cancelled under those limits. Completing that generation is the central material change explored in the delayed-treaty scenario.

evidence.note: Hood, Tiger and new designs are compared with the 35,000-ton limit.

segments.summary: Hood and the designs being developed after the war show why a limit suited to existing ships constrains their intended successors.

segments.title: British war debt and the limits of financial compulsion
segments.body: British debt in 1918 is about £7.8 billion, of which £1.28 billion is international and £6.52 billion internal. The total is roughly 140 percent of national GDP. American holdings account for a substantial part of the external debt. In this interpretation, that burden does not establish that Britain was compelled to abandon naval construction. Conditions after the Depression, the Second World War and the end of Lend-Lease should not be projected backwards onto 1918. France and Italy also faced heavy debts in circumstances that differed from the later postwar situation.

evidence.note: Debt totals and the distinction between the two postwar financial situations.

segments.summary: The debt argument distinguishes Britain after the First World War from its much later financial circumstances.

segments.title: Reading treaty decisions through contemporary evidence
segments.body: Treaty decisions need to be understood through contemporary evidence. Projecting later circumstances backwards can distort explanations of earlier choices. Seeking evidence only to reinforce an established thesis makes that problem worse. Reconstructing events in their contemporary sequence produces a more complicated account and preserves distinctions between the two postwar periods.

evidence.note: The methodological warning about backward projection and thesis-led evidence selection.

segments.summary: Projecting later financial conditions backwards can turn evidence into support for a conclusion chosen in advance.

segments.title: Budget surpluses and the promise of a land fit for heroes
segments.body: Governments wanted to fulfil postwar promises, including the British ambition of a land fit for heroes. British revenue in 1920-1921 was slightly above £1.4 billion and expenditure slightly below £1.2 billion, leaving a surplus of approximately £234 million. That money could support contingencies, capital infrastructure or faster debt repayment. In this interpretation, the surplus challenges a simple claim that Britain could no longer afford naval construction. Government finances also require a different analysis from the finances of an indebted business.

evidence.note: Revenue, expenditure, surplus and the uses of government surpluses.

segments.summary: British revenue, expenditure and social promises frame treaty participation as a choice about spending priorities.

segments.title: Why debt pressure can damage diplomatic influence
segments.body: A threat to call in debt can extract a concession while damaging the creditor relationship. The borrower has an incentive to repay quickly and avoid relying on that lender again. States can seek other countries or institutions for credit, giving them options an individual borrower may lack. Large debts also expose the creditor to the consequences of non-payment. These reciprocal interests make debt diplomacy politically complicated.

evidence.note: Creditor coercion, alternative lenders and reciprocal dependence.

segments.summary: Using debt to force a government into agreement can encourage repayment, distrust and a search for other lenders.

segments.title: Japan gains from war without the same debt burden
segments.body: Japan had comparatively little First World War debt. Its economy had weaknesses, but the war also brought gains, victories and military experience. Arms sales supplied several countries, including destroyers for France. Japan's position differed from that of the heavily indebted European powers. Its treaty participation therefore needs an explanation beyond a universal condition of financial exhaustion.

evidence.note: Japan’s debt position, gains and arms sales, including destroyers supplied to France.

segments.summary: Japan’s wartime gains and arms exports complicate explanations that reduce treaty participation to debt.

segments.title: Why naval parity with Italy constrains France
segments.body: Equality with France gives Italy a strategic advantage in this interpretation. Italy can concentrate against its remaining regional naval rival, while France has overseas commitments. Concentrating the French fleet in the Mediterranean leaves imperial defence exposed. Dispersing it overseas weakens the force available against Italy. The settlement consequently increases France's dependence on British naval support.

evidence.note: French imperial commitments and the strategic consequences of equality with Italy.

segments.summary: Equal naval allowances create unequal strategic demands when France must defend an empire as well as the Mediterranean.

segments.title: Ending the Anglo-Japanese alliance changes other relationships
segments.body: The United States wanted the Anglo-Japanese alliance to end because it did not want to face those navies' combined power. Greater French dependence on Britain creates a different strategic combination that could also concern American planners. This interpretation concerns increased naval reliance, without identifying a new formal alliance treaty. Congressional restrictions on spending remain another constraint on American naval power.

evidence.note: The American alliance concern and the interpretation of increased Anglo-French naval dependence.

segments.summary: Ending the Anglo-Japanese alliance removes one concern for America while greater French dependence on Britain creates another.

segments.title: Peace promises and a pause to absorb wartime lessons
segments.body: The treaty allows governments to present a visible commitment to peace between major powers. It also supports promises to direct money toward social and welfare programmes. Governments that prefer budget surpluses have another reason to welcome limits on naval expenditure. A more strategic rationale is a ten-year interval to digest wartime lessons before building the next generation. Industry and infrastructure would lose capacity during that pause and need attention before construction resumed. In this assessment, time to study wartime lessons is the strongest strategic case for the arrangement.

evidence.note: Domestic motivations and the planned interval for studying wartime experience.

segments.summary: The treaty offers political cover for spending cuts and time to study wartime experience before renewed construction.

segments.title: The arms race moves into treaty cruisers
segments.body: Capital-ship limits do not remove naval competition. Competition moves toward the most capable cruiser within roughly 10,000 tons standard displacement and eight-inch guns. The permitted category becomes a new focus for rivalry. This is an example of treaty rules redirecting competition between navies.

evidence.note: The continuing competition in 10,000-ton, eight-inch cruisers.

segments.summary: Restricting battleships shifts competition toward cruisers built around the 10,000-ton and eight-inch limits.

segments.title: Carrier limits force choices between hull numbers and capability
segments.body: Growing reliance on carrier aviation accompanies the move from grand-fleet operations toward task groups. Effective carriers need air groups, maintenance facilities, spares and enough protection to survive repeated operations. Losing a carrier quickly undermines a fleet that depends on its aircraft. A 27,000-ton ship could resemble Implacable, combining Illustrious-like protection with an Ark Royal-sized air group or better. A force of only five such ships would be insufficient for British sea communications and fleet support, with a similar numerical difficulty for the United States. Fitting more hulls within an aggregate tonnage allowance requires smaller carriers, forcing compromises between air-group size and protection. The resulting pressure helps explain attempts to compress useful carriers into about 10,000 tons.

evidence.note: Carrier survival, air-group requirements, the five-hull comparison and attempts at smaller designs.

segments.summary: A useful carrier needs aircraft capacity and protection, while fleet-wide tonnage limits restrict the number that can be built.

segments.title: Treaty extensions and different expectations of peace
segments.body: Repeated extensions preserve constraints beyond the intended breathing space. The interwar belief that war between major powers was over assumed that smaller opponents would be easy to defeat. The same assumption reappears in later claims that technological superiority leaves major powers facing only wars of choice, a misuse of the 'end of history' argument in this assessment. Experiences of the First World War differed: some sought permanent peace, while others regarded it as unfinished business, victory or opportunity. Governments also joined for different reasons, including saving money, redirecting expenditure and weakening military factions. A shared agreement therefore does not imply shared strategic assumptions.

evidence.note: Treaty extensions, major-power peace assumptions, criticism of misused 'end of history' arguments and differing reactions to World War I.

segments.summary: The treaty rests on expectations of lasting peace that governments and political factions do not share equally.

segments.title: How navies stretch treaty limits
segments.body: In this assessment, Italy treats treaty rules with particularly aggressive disregard. Other powers also manipulate the system. Britain uses water as armour, while the American Lexington carriers exceed their nominal weight. French experimentation includes cruiser submarines. Competition continues through efforts to obtain capability within and around the treaty framework.

evidence.note: Comparative treaty manipulation, British water protection and overweight Lexingtons.

segments.summary: Water used as protection and overweight Lexingtons illustrate the gap between numerical rules and competitive design practice.

segments.title: Italy’s advantage and France’s interrupted naval response
segments.body: France's wartime losses and trauma extend beyond the dead to the survivors of Verdun and the wider fighting on the Western Front. In this assessment, repeated government changes and distrust of the armed forces interrupt its naval response to Italy. Italy continues building ships and capability while France struggles to sustain its programmes. American treaty entitlement also exceeds what the navy can actually build, with Congressional authority and funding delayed until 1938. Those constraints support the judgment that Italy benefits most from the settlement.

evidence.note: French wartime damage and political instability, Italian building and the US funding comparison.

segments.summary: War losses, unstable governments and Congressional funding limits complicate claims about who benefits from the treaty.

segments.title: A seven-to-ten Japanese ratio and small capital ships
segments.body: Japan wants a seven-to-ten ratio rather than the smaller proportion accepted in the treaty. The proposed alternatives to Japan's actual 315,000-ton allowance are at least 350,000 and approximately 367,500 tons. A design exercise imagines three additional capital ships of about 17,000 tons each. Three Japanese equivalents of Dunkerque would provide one possible answer to those design constraints. This is an invitation to develop a counterfactual, rather than an identified Japanese construction programme.

evidence.note: Japan’s desired ratio and the speculative three-ship, 17,000-ton design exercise.

segments.summary: A larger Japanese allowance opens a speculative design exercise involving three small capital ships.

segments.title: Where historical counterfactuals hand over to wargaming
segments.body: The method develops an alternate situation from historical evidence far enough to provide a usable background. It stops when an argument begins depending on repeated layers of supposition. Wargaming then explores what follows from that initial position. Participants need to understand the historical systems represented and reason forward as the situation changes. The distinction limits how much confidence to place in later outcomes.

evidence.note: The stopping rule for historical extrapolation and the role of wargaming.

segments.summary: Historical evidence supplies a scenario’s starting conditions; successive layers of supposition mark the point for wargaming to take over.

segments.title: Failed negotiations leave ships as bargaining counters
segments.body: France could withdraw over equality with Italy, Japan over failure to obtain seven-to-ten, or Italy if denied equality with France. Negotiations could continue for years after an initial breakdown. During those talks, warships remain national-security assets and bargaining counters. The scenario consequently allows G3s, N3s, South Dakotas, Lexingtons, Amagis, Tosas, Kiis and No. 13 designs to be built. Building these ships would generate practical experience. The G3 provides a specific comparison with prewar capital ships: its design gives greater attention to aircraft threats and plunging fire. These outcomes depend on the proposed failure of the 1922 settlement.

evidence.note: Reasons for negotiating breakdown, continued building and the G3 design-generation comparison.

segments.summary: France, Japan or Italy could reject the proposed ratios while continuing negotiations and building the postwar designs.

segments.title: New capital ships accelerate retirement of older vessels
segments.body: New capital ships could cause older vessels to leave service sooner. Four British G3s are financially plausible in this scenario and their construction would create employment. Cruiser orders could continue alongside the capital-ship programme. The historical County-class programme provides a comparison for the scale of cruiser construction. Capital-ship orders might reduce cruiser numbers, while wider spending incentives could increase them, so the exact programme remains open.

evidence.note: Retirement of older ships, four possible G3s and uncertain parallel cruiser numbers.

segments.summary: Four G3s and accompanying cruiser orders could change the British fleet quickly, with the exact cruiser programme left open.

segments.title: Warship orders spread work across the economy
segments.body: British governments used naval procurement to stimulate employment. A warship needs steel, electrical cabling, boilers and turbines as well as furniture and toilets. Many trades and suppliers can therefore receive work from the same order. Spreading contracts across the country predates modern procurement politics. National governments can also arrange defence orders more directly than civilian infrastructure projects that require negotiations with local authorities.

evidence.note: The list of shipbuilding inputs and the comparison with local-government infrastructure administration.

segments.summary: Steel, machinery, fittings and furniture make warship construction a way to distribute employment across many trades and regions.

segments.title: Successor construction and pressure for 18-inch guns
segments.body: Five unrestricted years could permit follow-on classes after the G3, N3, South Dakota and Lexington programmes. The new American ships would create a strong battle line while older 14-inch battleships became candidates for retirement. British and Japanese 18-inch ships would affect later negotiations. They could also make an American preference for 16-inch guns harder to defend before Congress. The concern is that political comparison may favour a visibly larger weapon despite the Navy’s technical arguments.

evidence.note: Possible successor construction, older American ship retirement and Congressional reactions to rival gun sizes.

segments.summary: Five more years could bring successor designs as well as the cancelled ships, while rival 18-inch weapons create political pressure in America.

segments.title: Armour and subdivision in fast battleships and battlecruisers
segments.body: Completion of Italian Francesco Caracciolo ships could create another fast-battleship challenge for Britain. In this design interpretation, G3 and F3 designs approach fast battleships through the development of fully armoured battlecruisers. The distinction concerns subdivision as well as the amount and distribution of armour. A fully armoured battlecruiser retains battlecruiser subdivision beneath stronger protection. A fast battleship generally combines more subdivision with concentrated protection, often using an all-or-nothing arrangement. Such designs could make fast battleships more common during the five years before a settlement.

evidence.note: Possible Italian completion and the distinction between armour coverage and internal subdivision.

segments.summary: Stronger battlecruiser armour can coexist with internal subdivision different from that of a fast battleship.

segments.title: The tentative case for Admiral-class carrier conversions
segments.body: Dr. Clarke's doctoral research found internal documents treating Cammell Laird as experts in large strike carriers before the yard had built one. HMS Howe was the only suitable large hull he found that fitted the proposed timeline. That supports a possible Admiral-class conversion, without establishing that a carrier was completed. The exact dates when the unfinished Admiral-class ships left the stocks or were scrapped remain unresolved in this account. Eagle and Furious were conversions, while Hermes was new construction. An unfinished Admiral hull could provide a better foundation for a large carrier than Courageous or Glorious.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke's research account, the possible Howe conversion and uncertainty over unfinished Admiral hulls.

segments.summary: An archival reference to Cammell Laird’s carrier expertise prompts an inference about the unfinished Admiral-class hulls.

segments.title: British requirements for a large, survivable carrier
segments.body: British studies produced the figure of 27,000 tons standard displacement for a carrier capable of its intended duties. Requirements include a useful air group and survival against air threats in the Mediterranean and South China Sea. Planning anticipates a service life of twenty or thirty years. Treaty limits on both individual ships and aggregate carrier tonnage work against such large vessels. Anson and Howe could become carriers, while Rodney's treatment and a possible Ark Royal name remain speculative. Construction of the unfinished Admiral-class ships was suspended on 9 March 1917 and cancelled on 27 February 1919, although the hulls remained subjects for discussion.

evidence.note: The carrier study, service-life requirements, speculative conversions and Admiral programme dates.

segments.summary: British studies of a 27,000-ton carrier reflect air-group and protection requirements extending over a long service life.

segments.title: A new carrier based on the G3 hull form
segments.body: A G3 hull form could provide a starting point for a large, fast carrier. Fresh construction could proceed alongside the G3 battlecruisers. The illustrative carrier has twin islands. It could omit much of the capital-ship armour while retaining protection against cruiser gunfire, since a cruiser ambush was a concern for carriers. Its size would support enough fighters and strike aircraft for the intended tasks.

evidence.note: The hypothetical fresh-built G3-based carrier, twin islands and cruiser protection.

segments.summary: Fresh carrier construction could use a G3 hull design to provide size and speed without retaining the full battlecruiser armour scheme.

segments.title: Carrier fighters and the problem of warning before radar
segments.body: Fighters were important to carrier air groups in the first five or six years after the First World War. Without radar, warning could depend on observers in aircraft such as the Blackburn Blackburn spotting threats through binoculars and reporting by radio. A combat air patrol could still be in the wrong place or receive warning too late to intercept an attack. Those doubts encouraged emphasis on strike aircraft and machines capable of several tasks. The Swordfish combined torpedo attack, spotting and reconnaissance.

evidence.note: Visual warning, combat air patrol limitations and the Swordfish’s multiple roles.

segments.summary: Visual warning and uncertain interception help explain shifts toward strike aircraft and aircraft with several roles.

segments.title: TSR and the distinction between observation and identification
segments.body: In the 1930s and 1940s, TSR means torpedo, spotter and reconnaissance in contemporary naval usage. A different use of the abbreviation in the 1960s does not change that earlier meaning. The Royal Navy attempted to substitute recognizance for reconnaissance to distinguish positive recognition from less certain observation. The intended difference was between believing something was seen and knowing what had been identified. Attempts by admirals to introduce new vocabulary have a long history.

evidence.note: The earlier TSR expansion and the attempted reconnaissance/recognizance distinction.

segments.summary: TSR's contemporary expansion and a proposed distinction between reconnaissance and recognizance connect aircraft roles with confidence in identification.

segments.title: American and Japanese carriers without compulsory conversions
segments.body: G3s and Amagis could prompt American reconsideration of the lightly protected Lexington battlecruisers. Their intended scouting and trade-warfare roles help explain the light protection, but heavier foreign rivals could make that compromise less acceptable. Some hulls might become carriers, while new carrier designs could use the same general hull form. Tosa and Amagi ships in Japan could be completed in their intended capital-ship roles. Kaga would then lack its historical route into carrier service, and Japan would need another design or conversion source. The resulting carriers could reflect naval requirements more closely, with construction choices still uncertain.

evidence.note: The Lexington alternatives and the implications of completing Japanese capital ships.

segments.summary: Completing capital ships changes which hulls are available for American and Japanese carrier development.

segments.title: Carrier funding still depends on sea trade and politics
segments.body: The number and pace of carrier construction remain open questions. British sea trade and imperial commitments provide arguments for securing money after the recent experience of threatened maritime communications. Moffett and, later, King would still have to persuade Congress to fund American carriers. The absence of treaty limits creates design freedom without determining the funding outcome.

evidence.note: British sea-trade arguments and the continuing American Congressional funding challenge.

segments.summary: Removing treaty limits leaves the political problem of paying for enough carriers.

segments.title: Japanese carriers support attrition before decisive battle
segments.body: Japan could favour carrier construction in this scenario because carriers concentrate firepower with limited resources. Destroyers and torpedo boats offer comparable ways to offset an opponent's strength. Carriers suit the Japanese plan to wear down an approaching enemy before a decisive battle. Preparatory attrition reduces the enemy's strength and helps create favourable conditions for the main fleet engagement. Decisive battle therefore depends on other parts of naval doctrine, including attrition and the preference for large ships with large guns.

evidence.note: Carriers as an offset, preparatory attrition and the relationship to decisive battle.

segments.summary: Carriers fit an offset strategy that weakens the enemy before the main fleet engagement.

segments.title: Different carrier prospects for France and Italy
segments.body: In this scenario, Béarn would probably not become a carrier. France could instead finish some Normandie-class ships as battleships. It might build a separate carrier for imperial duties and policing. Italy could encounter political battles over securing a carrier.

evidence.note: The conditional Béarn, Normandie and Italian carrier outcomes.

segments.summary: France might pursue another carrier route while Italy faces domestic opposition to acquiring one.

segments.title: British six-inch and 9.2-inch cruiser possibilities
segments.body: The County design addressed features Britain disliked in the Hawkins class. Without the treaty ceiling, Britain could develop an enlarged continuation of the E-class light cruisers with twin six-inch turrets. A second, larger type might carry 9.2-inch guns. Both types could be built together. American cruiser construction would still depend on Congress and could remain close to the historical Omaha programme.

evidence.note: County and Hawkins comparison, E-class continuation and the possible British armament split.

segments.summary: Without the treaty ceiling, Britain could combine an enlarged light cruiser with a larger, more heavily armed type.

segments.title: Why Italy might finish Francesco Caracciolo ships
segments.body: Starting capital-ship design again would demand substantial effort and time, leaving Italy years behind the major powers. National pride could encourage completion of the existing Francesco Caracciolo programme. One or two completed ships are plausible, with completion of the whole class left uncertain. Their speed and reasonably good protection would retain value. They could remain useful even where a G3 probably offered stronger armour.

evidence.note: The schedule, prestige and capability arguments for conditional Caracciolo completion.

segments.summary: Completing existing designs could keep Italy from falling years behind while it starts a new programme.

segments.title: Italian cruisers for overseas presence
segments.body: Italy could seek ships that demonstrate national status and extend its presence abroad. Cruisers are suggested as the vessels for East Africa and other overseas duties. Capital ships could remain concentrated in the Mediterranean. That separation gives the two ship types different strategic roles in the proposed fleet.

evidence.note: Italian global-presence cruiser roles contrasted with Mediterranean capital-ship concentration.

segments.summary: Cruisers could carry Italy’s flag overseas while capital ships remain concentrated in the Mediterranean.

segments.title: Could 18-inch battleships leave room for 12-inch cruisers?
segments.body: Some navies could move toward 12-inch cruiser guns. Capital ships with much larger weapons would create more separation between those categories. An illustrative fleet pairs 18-inch capital ships with 12-inch and six-inch cruisers. Destroyer armament remains open. This is a possible development near the 1927 deadline, rather than an immediate or universal prediction.

evidence.note: The conditional calibre ladder and its placement near the 1927 deadline.

segments.summary: Larger capital-ship weapons could widen the distinction between battleships and heavily armed cruisers.

segments.title: Destroyer authorisation is separate from funding
segments.body: Congress could initially decide that the Wickes and Clemson programmes provide enough destroyers. New classes appearing in foreign fleets might later create pressure to fund more ships. Some vessels built in the 1930s had been authorised under First World War procurement arrangements. Their funding had remained a separate legislative step. Later construction could therefore proceed by funding an existing authorisation.

evidence.note: Foreign-class pressure and the distinction between ship authorisation and later funding.

segments.summary: The Wickes and Clemson programmes could delay new American destroyers until foreign construction changes Congressional priorities.

segments.title: Cruiser submarines promise a cheaper commerce-warfare offset
segments.body: Cruiser submarines could receive more investment without the treaty system. They appear to offer a surface cruiser's commerce-warfare capability at lower cost. Submergence promises greater survivability and makes the design attractive on paper. In this assessment, those apparent advantages would still fail to make it operationally viable. Governments could nevertheless pursue the concept because its promised economy and ability to hide seem appealing.

evidence.note: The cost, commerce-warfare and submergence arguments attracting cruiser-submarine investment.

segments.summary: Apparent savings and the ability to hide could attract cruiser-submarine orders despite poor operational prospects.

segments.title: Difficult submarine designs can advance ordinary submarines
segments.body: Making cruiser submarines work demands unusually complicated engineering. The attempt could develop technologies that also improve ordinary submarines. Nations that neither pursue the research nor build comparable fleets could fall further behind, especially Germany and the Soviet Union in this scenario. Those research benefits do not depend on cruiser submarines becoming effective warships. The vessels themselves would have little operational value beyond unusual, specific circumstances in this assessment.

evidence.note: Engineering complexity, ordinary-submarine benefits and countries falling behind.

segments.summary: Engineering complicated cruiser submarines could create useful technologies even when the completed vessels have little value.

segments.title: Gunfire can turn a cruiser submarine into a trapped surface vessel
segments.body: In this assessment, a hundred cruiser submarines armed with six-inch guns could not win the Second World War. Convoy escorts with guns as small as four inches could damage their pressure hulls and prevent diving. A damaged submarine would then remain exposed on the surface, where a destroyer could engage it. The destroyer's more stable gun platform improves its chance of hitting, while the submarine has no armour. An enemy able to escort convoys and exploit that vulnerability undermines the proposed raiding fleet's advantage.

evidence.note: The hypothetical mass cruiser-submarine proposal and the pressure-hull damage mechanism.

segments.summary: Damage to an unarmoured pressure hull can remove a submarine’s ability to dive and expose it to a steadier destroyer gun platform.

segments.title: Fast minelayers remain a postwar priority
segments.body: Minelaying was an important part of First World War naval operations. Fast minelayers remain desirable to many navies. Continued attention to that requirement is therefore expected during the unrestricted period. The demand follows from wartime experience, with no particular class or construction schedule specified.

evidence.note: The stated wartime importance of mines and demand for fast minelayers.

segments.summary: The importance of minelaying in the First World War supports further work on fast minelayers.

segments.title: Shipyard investment also equips civilian builders
segments.body: Naval infrastructure investment can put money into local economies. Shipyard projects require machinery such as diggers and tractors and can improve construction firms’ capabilities. That equipment remains after the naval project ends. Civilian contractors can use it for roads, housing and factories. Naval investment can therefore contribute to wider postwar economic rebuilding through equipment and skills.

evidence.note: The movement of construction machinery from shipyard work into later civilian projects.

segments.summary: Machinery acquired for shipyard construction can later help civilian firms build roads, houses and factories.

segments.title: A race for better ships within political budgets
segments.body: The projected naval race would focus on improving ship designs. Governments lack the appetite and budgets for a large expansion in numbers. Completed South Dakotas, Colorados and Lexingtons would already give America a substantial fleet, comparable as a baseline to Britain's mass of 15-inch-gun ships. Congress is unlikely to fund another dozen capital ships once those programmes are complete. Successive designs could therefore improve while further expansion remains politically constrained.

evidence.note: The qualitative-race forecast and the Congressional limit after existing programmes are completed.

segments.summary: Completing large existing programmes does not imply that Congress will fund an unlimited increase in capital-ship numbers.

segments.title: Germany’s naval race competes with the army’s budget
segments.body: In this interpretation, the Imperial German Navy's reluctance to drive technological change follows a budget calculation: more advanced ships cost more. Once existing allocations cannot cover those costs, naval leaders must seek extra money. The army treats that request as competition for its own allocation. Britain's combination of expensive ships and substantial numbers takes the race beyond the funding the German navy can secure. Technical ability alone does not remove that financial constraint.

evidence.note: The cost escalation and army-budget explanation of Germany’s inability to match Britain.

segments.summary: Rising British ship costs put German naval ambitions into conflict with the army’s claims on funding.

segments.title: Different national motives sustain competition in better warships
segments.body: Japan seeks larger and better ships because it cannot sustain the same fleet numbers as rival powers. Making an opponent commit its whole fleet supports a deterrent strategy. Italy combines capable naval architects and a preference for ongoing construction with the ambition to dominate the Mediterranean. The United States brings the prestige of a rising power and confidence in its industry. Britain treats naval strength as the foundation of security and international influence. These motives sustain competition within the political limits on fleet expansion.

evidence.note: The sequence of Japanese, Italian, American and British reasons for naval competition.

segments.summary: Japan’s numerical disadvantage, Italian Mediterranean ambitions and Anglo-American confidence in naval power support continued design competition.

segments.title: What follows G3, N3 and No. 13?
segments.body: How far successor classes progress before a treaty in 1927 would determine which ships could be built. Britain's likely successor to G3 and N3 is a fast battleship with at least 18-inch guns. The precise combination of technology remains open. Japanese planning already includes 18-inch and larger weapons and the No. 13 designs. The next American design and the Italian successor to Francesco Caracciolo remain unspecified.

evidence.note: The uncertain next generation, British fast-battleship prediction and Japanese gun plans.

segments.summary: Successor classes become the uncertain part of the scenario once the cancelled designs have been completed.

segments.title: Coolidge, naval aviation and warships as industrial orders
segments.body: The naval secretary serving under Coolidge wanted to enlarge the fleet and develop its aviation capability. In this comparison, Calvin Coolidge was more concerned with domestic politics than Harding. Warship construction offered a means of influencing industrial production. His version of laissez-faire economics allowed government to place orders while avoiding direct management of industry. These leadership differences add another variable to a treaty delayed until 1927.

evidence.note: The unnamed secretary's fleet interest and Coolidge's use of orders within his version of laissez-faire economics.

segments.summary: A different American administration changes the political and industrial setting for negotiations in 1927.

segments.title: Britain’s 1927 cabinet and competing defence choices
segments.body: Baldwin's government includes Churchill as chancellor and Neville Chamberlain as minister of health. In this critical assessment, Churchill shifts between cutting and increasing defence spending and bears some responsibility for inadequate funding of Singapore. His changes to Indian railway oversight also restrict the government's ability to add lines. Churchill was not prime minister in 1939 and could not exercise that office's authority over peace proposals. William Clive Bridgeman is First Lord of the Admiralty and Austen Chamberlain is foreign secretary. These personalities and spending choices form part of the changed 1927 negotiating environment.

evidence.note: Cabinet roles, the Singapore and railway criticisms, and Churchill’s lack of prime-ministerial authority in 1939.

segments.summary: The cabinet discussion connects naval policy with Churchill’s spending choices, Singapore and Indian railway oversight.

segments.title: Ship orders generate tax receipts and protect employment
segments.body: Continued naval orders could keep money moving through the British economy. Yards and suppliers employ workers whose income and spending create taxable activity. The chain extends through companies supplying goods and services to shipbuilding. Orders also sustain constituencies dependent on yard employment. In this political explanation, Town-class names and the placement of construction orders tied cruisers to constituencies where shipyard employment made cancellation costly. Those orders survived. Employment and tax receipts provide incentives for those orders, although the amount returned in tax is not quantified.

evidence.note: Taxable employment and supply chains, followed by the Town-class naming and constituency explanation.

segments.summary: Shipyard wages and supplier orders circulate money through the economy and create constituencies with reasons to resist cancellation.

segments.title: A 1927 treaty based on construction quotas
segments.body: Governments could still want agreement in 1927 to prevent competition getting out of hand. The proposed mechanism controls the next generation after the ships already ordered. It limits construction over a period instead of total fleet tonnage. Illustrative proportions could allow France and Italy five ships, Japan seven, and Britain and America ten. Japan’s preference for large ships would complicate such numerical ratios. A one-in, one-out replacement requirement is another possibility.

evidence.note: The hypothetical construction-rate settlement, illustrative ratios and replacement rule.

segments.summary: A later settlement could limit new ships over an agreed period and require an older ship to leave for each replacement.

segments.title: Existing large ships change a later displacement ceiling
segments.body: Ships of about 45,000 tons standard displacement or more would already exist in the scenario. A later treaty might consequently use a ceiling such as 50,000 tons. That is an illustrative figure, rather than a settled provision. The difference from 35,000 tons changes what designers can accommodate in a battleship. Older ships would still be candidates for disposal. In this forecast, a new battleship could not match two contemporary large capital ships.

evidence.note: Existing large ships and the illustrative 50,000-versus-35,000-ton comparison.

segments.summary: A world already containing 45,000-ton capital ships would negotiate from a different starting point.

segments.title: Twenty ships on paper do not mean twenty available
segments.body: One possible settlement gives Britain and America twenty capital ships each and Japan fourteen. Japan would be unlikely to accept twelve if its insistence on a seven-to-ten ratio caused the original negotiations to break down. The larger fleets seek an advantage in ships available for operations. Roughly one-third may be in refit or maintenance, with others training or in transit. The illustrative available totals are about twelve from twenty and eight or nine from fourteen. France's and Italy's allowances would also affect Japanese demands and the resulting Anglo-American totals.

evidence.note: The hypothetical fleet limits and approximate operational-availability calculations.

segments.summary: Possible twenty-to-fourteen fleet totals are explained through refits, training and the need for an operational advantage.

segments.title: A decade of continuous construction in improving pairs
segments.body: The agreement could cover carriers and cruisers alongside capital ships. Submarine restrictions are less likely in this forecast because governments would resist surrendering large forces. A treaty running from 1927 to 1937 could permit continuous building. Ten capital ships during the decade would be affordable for either Britain or America in this estimate. Orders might come in pairs, with each batch incorporating improvements over the previous one.

evidence.note: Possible treaty categories, the ten-year term and construction in successive pairs.

segments.summary: A hypothetical 1927-1937 settlement could regulate carriers and cruisers while allowing steady capital-ship construction.

segments.title: Replacement arithmetic leaves little room for older battleships
segments.body: Britain's eight G3s and N3s combined with ten later ships would yield eighteen newer capital ships. Hood would bring that total to nineteen within a possible ceiling of twenty. Very few First World War veterans could remain in that battle fleet. America's Colorados, South Dakotas and Lexingtons would account for sixteen ships before another ten entered service. Some Colorados could leave before the 1940s if a twenty-ship limit were enforced. The arithmetic depends on the scenario's assumed construction and fleet ceilings.

evidence.note: British and American fleet-renewal arithmetic under hypothetical limits.

segments.summary: Eight British G3s and N3s plus ten later ships would fill most of an illustrative twenty-ship fleet.

segments.title: Continuous building leaves more room to experiment with layouts
segments.body: The historical North Carolina design is used as a comparison rather than a forecast. Later ships in this scenario might share some features while differing substantially in others. Continuous construction could encourage further experiments with all-forward or all-aft armament. Those routes remain possibilities, with no completed alternative design specified.

evidence.note: The North Carolina comparison and possible all-forward or all-aft armament experiments.

segments.summary: The counterfactual fleet need not reproduce historical battleship designs if successive classes keep testing different layouts.

segments.title: Yamato’s historical design loses its intended opponents
segments.body: In this scenario, Yamato would not appear in its historical form after the No. 13 ships had been built. In this interpretation of its design concept, it would defeat one older American standard battleship while holding another off. That comparison becomes obsolete if those ships have already been replaced. Queen Elizabeths, R-class ships and older French, Italian and Japanese vessels would also be unlikely to remain in primary service by the late 1930s. Changed opponents would give Japan different design requirements.

evidence.note: The Yamato prediction, the two-opponent concept and disappearance of the older fleets.

segments.summary: Replacing older standard battleships changes the comparison behind the familiar Yamato design.

segments.title: Deutschland’s raiding role and gun arrangement under stronger opposition
segments.body: If Germany follows a broadly similar political trajectory, Deutschland faces G3s, Lexingtons, Amagis and their successors. Its long-range raiding role makes little sense against that opposition in this assessment, and coastal defence is a suggested alternative. Its six 11-inch guns in two separated triple turrets resemble the pre-dreadnoughts being replaced. Concentrating the armament forward is proposed as a better way to use those six guns and improve fire control. The preferred minimum useful battery is nine 11-inch guns. Treaty constraints help explain the historical choice, while leaving room for criticism of the arrangement.

evidence.note: The conditional raider/coastal-defence comparison and criticism of six guns in separated turrets.

segments.summary: A stronger world battle fleet raises doubts about Deutschland’s long-range role and prompts criticism of its divided gun battery.

segments.title: Scharnhorst loses its escape margin against numerous fast battleships
segments.body: In this assessment, Scharnhorst was the best fast battleship Germany could build at the time. Its 11-inch guns would face ships with 16.5-inch or 18-inch weapons in the scenario. A speed above 28 knots provides a narrower advantage when numerous opponents can also exceed 28 knots. Damage that reduces speed could remove the ability to escape.

evidence.note: Scharnhorst’s armament, similarly fast opponents and the effect of damage on escape.

segments.summary: High speed is less reassuring when many opponents are also fast and carry much heavier guns.

segments.title: Continuous orders preserve a base for industrial expansion
segments.body: Britain, America, Italy, France and Japan would enter the 1930s with a stronger industrial base after continued construction. Production would still be well below First World War levels. Continued investment and orders would prevent the same deep trough in activity. Trained workers, infrastructure and working production methods would remain available. Expanding that functioning capacity for an emergency would be easier than recreating it before urgent demand could be met.

evidence.note: The reduced industrial trough and advantages of expanding existing capacity.

segments.summary: A working shipbuilding industry can expand for emergencies more readily than one rebuilt after a long shortage of orders.

segments.title: Larger carrier development changes the Yorktown path
segments.body: Four or five capital-ship generations could emerge over twenty years of construction. They would develop alongside growing air power and substantial carriers. In this forecast, the historical Yorktown class would not appear. American carriers could instead approach the Midway concept, combining extensive protection with a large air group. The comparison concerns desired capabilities and does not specify a reproduction of the historical Midway design.

evidence.note: The ship-generation forecast and the conceptual Yorktown/Midway comparison.

segments.summary: Repeated construction alongside growing air power could lead to carriers with more armour and larger air groups.

segments.title: Built fleets make strength visible without guaranteeing peace
segments.body: Rival construction makes national technological and industrial strength visible in ships actually built and serving. Japan would have to respond to the larger carrier and capital-ship environment. Governments could feel more confident while judging their opponents more realistically. Visible strength would still give no guarantee of peace. Britain and France could take a more assertive approach to Hitler's rise because usable capability would already exist.

evidence.note: Visible national capabilities, the rejected guarantee of peace and the conditional diplomatic effect.

segments.summary: Continuous construction makes industrial capability visible and could give Britain and France stronger options during Hitler’s rise.

segments.title: Wealth and industrial potential take time to become capability
segments.body: Wealth does not supply an immediate operational fleet. Some interpretations of the 'end of history' argument can encourage the assumption that purchasing power already amounts to military capability. Procurement takes years, and people need training before the equipment can be used effectively. Confidence based on industrial potential can therefore overstate available strength. An opponent with trained, existing capability can expose that weakness. The resulting fear can encourage irrational choices and contribute to war.

evidence.note: Procurement and training delays, the 'end of history' criticism and fear arising from false confidence in military strength.

segments.summary: Orders, delivery and crew training separate the ability to pay for equipment from the ability to use it.

segments.title: Japanese fear, stronger opponents and the smaller-war forecast
segments.body: In this interpretation, the faction pressing Japan toward war believed it was losing the peace and faced destruction of its culture. It expected probable defeat in war while still seeing a small chance of success that peace did not offer. Visible rival construction could undermine even that calculation. A ship intended to fight two older American standard battleships would face a different task against two N3s or South Dakotas because those opponents are heavily protected. The counterfactual forecast is a series of smaller wars instead of a world war. Italy's relationship with Germany remains uncertain.

evidence.note: The Japanese faction’s perceived predicament, heavily protected opponents and the uncertain smaller-war conclusion.

segments.summary: Visible rival construction could change the Japanese pro-war faction's belief that war offered its only chance of success.

segments.title: A possible 2,500- to 3,000-ton destroyer
segments.body: Destroyers in the projected fleets could reach around 2,500 tons standard displacement. That would be sufficient for a very good destroyer in this design estimate. A ship with eight guns in four twin turrets and ten torpedoes could approach 3,000 tons. These figures are a speculative design sketch rather than the specification of an ordered class.

evidence.note: The conditional displacement, gun and torpedo estimate for destroyers.

segments.summary: The closing design sketch suggests larger destroyers, with extra displacement for eight guns and ten torpedoes.

segments.title: New orders could remove First World War ships from primary roles
segments.body: In this forecast, no First World War ships would remain in Britain's primary fleet roles by 1939. Reserve survival remains possible if permitted by the agreement, but is doubtful. New construction would reduce the need to modernize older ships. Hood might be the oldest remaining capital ship and could herself be replaced. If treaty restrictions ended in 1937, Britain could order another four or five ships. Preserved infrastructure would allow faster construction than the historical King George V programme. Hood and any surviving Warspite could consequently leave service by 1939, although their individual survival is uncertain.

evidence.note: The primary-role prediction, reserve caveat and conditional post-1937 replacement of Hood and Warspite.

segments.summary: Continued building reduces dependence on modernized veterans and could replace even Hood after a treaty expires.

segments.title: Warspite’s machinery helps explain its modernization
segments.body: One explanation for Warspite's early modernization starts with its distinctive as-built combination of boilers and turbines. In this assessment, that machinery gave it different and, in several respects, better performance than its sisters. Its performance helps explain both the priority and form of its modernization. First World War damage was another influence on those decisions. The machinery comparison remains general, without models, equipment counts or performance figures.

evidence.note: The machinery distinction, performance assessment and combined reasons for modernization.

segments.summary: Warspite's distinctive as-built boiler and turbine combination provides one explanation for its early modernization.
